T1.name: Choosing the wrong relationship or reversing a division
T1.example: For 120 km in 2 hours, calculate speed as 120 × 2 = 240. Use distance ÷ time = 60 km/h. For time, use distance ÷ speed, not the reverse.

T2.name: Treating minutes as hundredths of an hour

T3.name: Reading decimal hours as clock minutes
T3.example: Read 1.5 hours as 1 hour 50 minutes (or 1 hour 5 minutes). The fractional hour is 0.5 × 60 = 30 minutes.

T4.name: Calculating with one unit but labelling the result with another
T4.example: 120 km ÷ 90 minutes = 1.33… km/min, labelled as km/h. Convert the rate by multiplying by 60, or divide by 1.5 hours, to obtain 80 km/h.

T5.name: Combining the whole journey's distance with only part of its time, or vice versa
T5.example: Travel 30 km in 1 hour, then 120 km in 2 hours; calculate 150 ÷ 2 = 75 km/h. The matching totals are 150 km and 3 hours, giving 50 km/h.

T6.name: Omitting a stop when the requested average includes it
T6.example: Travel 120 km in 2 moving hours with an additional 30-minute stop; give 60 km/h for the whole journey including the stop. Use 120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h.

T7.name: Taking an unweighted mean of speeds when time at each speed differs
T7.example: One hour at 30 km/h and two hours at 60 km/h: (30 + 60) ÷ 2 = 45. Total distance ÷ total time gives 150 ÷ 3 = 50 km/h.

T8.name: Rounding an intermediate conversion/calculation too early
T8.example: Convert 20 minutes to 0.33 hours, then calculate 10 ÷ 0.33 = 30.30 km/h. Retain 20/60 hours to obtain 30 km/h, then round only the requested final result.
